---
title: "Cleaning and tidying medical data"
---

Before you can model data, it has to be tidy and clean:
one row per observation,
one column per variable,
and values coded the way you'll analyze them.
In class, we'll do one exercise that reshapes data into a tidy shape,
and one that recodes numbers into categories we can read.
For more practice,
see [Extra practice: cleaning and tidying](07-practice-clean-and-tidy.qmd).

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(medicaldata)
```

## Exercise 1: Gum health over the trial's visits

`opt` (from `medicaldata`) is the Obstetrics and Periodontal Therapy trial:
pregnant women with periodontal disease were randomized
to periodontal treatment (`T`) or control (`C`)
([Michalowicz et al., 2006](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa062249)).
Their gums were examined at baseline (`BL`), visit 3 (`V3`), and visit 5 (`V5`).
We'll look at two of the measures:
the gingival index (`GE`, where higher means more inflamed gums)
and the average pocket depth in millimetres (`PD.avg`).

Every dataset in `medicaldata` is a base R data frame, not a tibble,
so printing one prints every row.
We'll use [`head()`](https://search.r-project.org/R/refmans/utils/html/head.html)
to print just the first 6.

```{r}
gums <- opt |>
  select(PID, Group, BL.GE, BL.PD.avg, V3.GE, V3.PD.avg, V5.GE, V5.PD.avg)
head(gums)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Your turn

A header like `V3.PD.avg` packs two variables into one name:
the visit (`V3`) and the measure (`PD.avg`).
`PD.avg` has a dot of its own,
so `names_sep = "."` would split it in the wrong place.
The `names_pattern` below reads "the visit, a dot, then the rest".

1. Pivot the six measure columns into `visit`, `measure`, and `value`,
   dropping missing values.
2. Pivot `measure` back out, so `GE` and `PD.avg` are their own columns.
   Call the result `gums_tidy`.
3. Calculate the mean pocket depth and gingival index
   for each group at each visit.
   What happened to the treatment group's gums?
4. Plot the mean pocket depth at each visit, coloured by group.

```{r}
#| eval: false
gums_tidy <- gums |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = ____,
    names_to = c(____, ____),
    names_pattern = "(BL|V3|V5)\\.(.*)",
    values_to = "value",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = ____, values_from = ____)

gums_summary <- gums_tidy |>
  group_by(____, ____) |>
  summarize(
    avg_pd = mean(PD.avg, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_ge = mean(GE, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

ggplot(gums_summary, aes(x = visit, y = ____, colour = ____, group = ____)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
```
:::

## Exercise 2: Coded variables

`blood_storage` (from `medicaldata`) follows 316 men
who received blood transfusions during radical prostatectomy
([Cata et al., 2011](https://higgi13425.github.io/medicaldata/reference/blood_storage.html)).
Its categories are stored as numbers:

```{r}
blood_storage |>
  count(RBC.Age.Group, Recurrence)
```

- `Recurrence`: 0 = no, 1 = yes
  (biochemical recurrence of prostate cancer)
- `RBC.Age.Group`: storage age of the transfused red blood cells,
  in terciles: 1 = younger, 2 = middle, 3 = older

::: {.callout-note}
## Your turn

Make `blood`:
add `recurrence`, a factor with labels `no` and `yes`,
and `rbc_age_group`, a factor with labels `younger`, `middle` and `older`.
Then count `rbc_age_group` by `recurrence`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
blood <- blood_storage |>
  mutate(
    recurrence = factor(Recurrence, levels = ____, labels = ____),
    rbc_age_group = factor(RBC.Age.Group, levels = ____, labels = ____)
  )

blood |>
  count(____, ____)
```
:::

You'll model `blood` in [Logistic regression](05-logistic-regression.qmd).
